title: United Kingdom | UK GDPR, Data Protection and Operational Resilience for Banks
tagline: Protect UK customers' data and services: UK GDPR, the DPA 2018, the 2025 reforms, breach notification and PRA/FCA resilience rules.
sectors: Contact centres and operations teams in UK banks
Technology, cyber security and resilience teams in UK banks
description:
A UK-specific quest on protecting customer data and keeping banking services running. It is based on the **UK GDPR** and the **Data Protection Act 2018**, as amended by the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025** (including recognised legitimate interests, new subject access and automated decision rules and the **section 164A** complaints duty in force since 19 June 2026), enforced by the **Information Commission**, which replaced the Information Commissioner on 30 September 2026. It also covers the **PRA and FCA operational resilience** rules and the incident and third-party reporting regime in **FCA PS26/2** and **PRA PS7/26**, which applies from 18 March 2027.

UK GDPR Article 39 makes awareness-raising and training of staff who process data part of the DPO's tasks, and the regulators expect staff to recognise, escalate and report breaches and incidents quickly. The quest is for everyone who handles customer data in a UK bank, with extra depth for incident, resilience and complaints teams. It uses real FCA and PRA enforcement cases.

It builds knowledge of the UK framework and does not replace your bank's own policies, procedures or role-specific training.
audience: Branch, contact-centre and operations staff in UK banks who handle customer data every day
Customer relations and complaints staff handling rights requests and data protection complaints
Technology, cyber security and incident management teams
Business service owners and resilience teams working on important business services
Data protection officers, compliance staff and senior managers, including SMF24 teams
outcomes: Explain the UK GDPR, the DPA 2018, the 2025 Act and the roles of the Information Commission, FCA and PRA
Apply the Article 5 principles and choose the right lawful basis, including recognised legitimate interests
Protect customer confidentiality and avoid the DPA 2018 section 170 offence
Handle rights requests, automated decision safeguards and section 164A complaints on the correct timelines
Resist social engineering and run the Article 33 and 34 breach process
Apply impact tolerances and the 2027 FCA/PRA incident and third-party reporting rules

quest.name: The Harrowfield Resilience Week
quest.premise: You have just joined the Data Protection and Resilience office of Harrowfield Bank plc, a UK bank headquartered in Leeds with a contact centre in Edinburgh and branches across the country. In one week you face a misdirected customer list, a suspicious police email, a furious data subject, a phished mailbox and a payments outage. With DPO Nadia Hussain, resilience head Kwame Mensah, contact-centre lead Eilidh Campbell, cyber analyst Tomasz Nowak and COO Helen Ashworth, clear five stages, then face the final boss: the regulators' questions.

badge.name: UK Data and Resilience Guardian
badge.description: Awarded to bank staff who can apply UK data protection law and PRA/FCA operational resilience and incident rules with confidence.

sessions.title: The UK Data Rulebook: UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and the Principles
sessions.summary: Map the UK framework (UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and the new Information Commission), learn the key terms and apply the seven principles to everyday banking.
objectives: Describe the UK GDPR, the DPA 2018, the 2025 Act and the role of the Information Commission, FCA and PRA
Recognise personal data, special category data, controllers and processors in a bank
Apply the six Article 5 principles and the accountability principle to banking situations
Explain why outsourcing or intra-group transfers do not move the controller's responsibility

cards.title: Day one: the spreadsheet on the train
cards.setting: Data Protection Office, Harrowfield Bank plc, Leeds. Monday, 8:40 am.

lines.text: Your visitor pass is still warm from the printer when a message flashes across the team screen: 'URGENT: laptop left on the 07:12 to York'.

Welcome to Harrowfield. I'm Nadia Hussain, the bank's Data Protection Officer. Your quest starts now: by Friday you will know the UK data and resilience rules well enough to explain them to a regulator.
Nadia, it's Eilidh in Edinburgh. One of my contact-centre agents emailed a customer list to her personal address so she could 'work on it at home'. 2,300 names, account numbers and phone numbers.
Tomasz from cyber security. And the laptop on the York train belongs to a mortgage adviser. It's encrypted, but nobody knows yet whether the screen was locked.
Two incidents before coffee. Before we decide what to do, our new colleague needs the map: which UK laws apply, who the regulators are and what 'personal data' really means.
So: what is the UK rulebook for customer data, and what principles does every person in this bank have to live by? That is Stage 1.

cards.title: The UK data rulebook in five pieces

scenes.heading: UK GDPR
scenes.narration: The UK kept the EU's General Data Protection Regulation after Brexit and adapted it. It sets the principles, the lawful bases, people's rights and the security and breach duties.

scenes.heading: Data Protection Act 2018
scenes.narration: The 2018 Act sits beside the UK GDPR. It adds UK exemptions and conditions, the regulator's powers, fines and criminal offences, such as obtaining or disclosing personal data without the controller's consent.

scenes.heading: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
scenes.narration: The 2025 Act amended both. It added recognised legitimate interests, new rules on automated decisions and subject access, and a duty for organisations to handle data protection complaints themselves.

scenes.heading: The Information Commission
scenes.narration: On 30 September 2026 the Information Commission took over from the Information Commissioner. It enforces data protection law, handles complaints and can fine. Older documents still say ICO.

scenes.heading: FCA and PRA
scenes.narration: For banks, data security is also a conduct and prudential matter. The FCA and the PRA expect sound systems and controls, and they have fined firms for cyber and IT failures.

cards.title: Who answers for customer data at Harrowfield
cards.caption: The controller carries the legal duty, but every layer has a part to play.

items.label: The bank as controller
items.detail: Decides why and how customer data is used, and must be able to prove it complies.

items.label: Board and senior managers
items.detail: Set policy, fund controls and own the risk under the SM&CR.

items.label: Data Protection Officer
items.detail: Advises, monitors compliance and leads awareness and training.

items.label: Processors and suppliers
items.detail: Act only on the bank's written instructions.

items.label: Every member of staff
items.detail: Handles data only as the bank instructs and reports problems fast.

cards.title: Key words you must get right
cards.body:
**Personal data** is any information about an identified or identifiable living person: a name, an account number, an IP address, a voice recording, even a note about a customer's mood.

- **Processing** is almost anything you do with it: collecting, storing, viewing, sharing, deleting.
- **Controller**: the organisation that decides the purposes and means. Harrowfield is the controller of its customer data.
- **Processor**: a firm that processes data for the controller, such as a cloud provider or a mailing house.
- **Special category data**: health, ethnic origin, religion, biometrics used for identification and similar sensitive types. It needs an extra condition and extra care.

In a bank, nearly every customer record is personal data, so the rules apply to nearly everything you touch.

cards.question: A customer's mobile number is held in the CRM with no name next to it, but it can be linked to the account through the phone banking log. Is it personal data?
options: Yes, because the person can be identified by linking it with other information the bank holds
No, because personal data must include a name
Only if the customer has given consent to its use
cards.explanation: Information is personal data if a living person can be identified from it directly or indirectly, including by combining it with other data the bank holds. A name is not required, and consent has nothing to do with the definition.

cards.title: The seven principles of UK GDPR Article 5
cards.caption: Article 5(2) adds the seventh: accountability. The controller must be able to demonstrate compliance with all six.

items.label: Lawful, fair, transparent
items.detail: Have a lawful basis, treat people fairly and tell them what you do.

items.label: Purpose limitation
items.detail: Collect for clear purposes; do not reuse in incompatible ways.

items.label: Data minimisation
items.detail: Only what is adequate, relevant and necessary.

items.label: Accuracy
items.detail: Keep it right and fix errors without delay.

items.label: Storage limitation
items.detail: Keep it identifiable no longer than needed.

items.label: Integrity and confidentiality
items.detail: Keep it secure against misuse, loss and damage.

cards.title: Principle meets practice
cards.prompt: Match each Harrowfield habit to the principle it puts into practice.

pairs.right: The loan form no longer asks for marital status, because the credit model does not use it.
Closed-account records are deleted when the retention schedule says their purpose has ended.
A returned letter triggers an address check before the next statement is sent.
The bank keeps records of processing and evidence of who was trained and when.
Data collected for fraud checks is not passed to the marketing team for campaigns.
Customer files are encrypted and access is limited to staff who need them.

cards.title: The turn: 'we'll just keep everything'

lines.text: I'm Helen Ashworth, Chief Operating Officer. Nadia, the new analytics platform team wants to load every customer record since 2005. Storage is cheap. Why not?
Because cheap storage doesn't make it lawful. Old data we no longer need is a liability: if it leaks, we answer for every record.
Kwame, operational resilience. And more data means a bigger blast radius in a cyber attack. We'd be enlarging the target.
So what do I tell the project team?
Tell them to define the purpose, take only the fields they need and follow the retention schedule. Then we document the decision. That's accountability in one sentence.

cards.title: The analytics data load
cards.situation: The analytics team wants every customer record since 2005, including closed accounts, to 'see what patterns emerge'. No purpose has been written down, and some records are past their retention date. Helen asks you, as the DPO's analyst, what to advise.

choices.text: Advise defining a specific purpose first, loading only necessary fields, excluding data past retention, and recording the assessment and decision
choices.outcome: Best answer. This applies purpose limitation, minimisation and storage limitation, and the written record lets the bank demonstrate compliance, as accountability requires.

choices.text: Approve the load but restrict access to the analytics team
choices.outcome: Access controls help security, but they do not cure the lack of a purpose or the retention of data that should have been deleted.

choices.text: Approve the load because the bank already holds the data lawfully
choices.outcome: Holding data lawfully for one purpose does not make a new, undefined use lawful, and keeping expired data breaches storage limitation.

choices.text: Refuse all analytics projects that use customer data
choices.outcome: Too blunt. Analytics can be lawful with a defined purpose, a lawful basis and proper safeguards. The job is to make it compliant, not to ban it.

cards.title: Real case: Equifax Ltd, fined by the FCA (2023)
cards.body:
In October 2023 the FCA fined **Equifax Ltd** about **GBP 11.2m** over the 2017 cyber attack on its US parent company.

- Hackers reached the personal data of roughly **13.8 million UK consumers**, because Equifax Ltd sent UK data to its parent's servers in the US for processing.
- The FCA found Equifax Ltd had **not treated the arrangement as outsourcing**, so it did not oversee how the data was protected, despite known weaknesses in the parent's security.
- It learned that UK data was affected about **six weeks** after the parent discovered the hack.

**The lesson for Harrowfield:** sending data to a group company or supplier does not hand over responsibility. The controller must know where its data is, who protects it and how, and be able to show that it checked.

cards.title: Myth or fact?

cards.front: 'If we got the data lawfully, we can use it for anything.'
cards.back: Myth. Purpose limitation means new uses must be compatible with the original purpose or have their own lawful basis.

cards.front: 'Data protection only applies to digital records.'
cards.back: Myth. Paper files in a structured filing system are covered too, and so are recorded calls.

cards.front: 'The DPO is personally liable for breaches.'
cards.back: Myth. The controller, the bank, carries the legal duty. The DPO advises and monitors.

cards.front: 'Accountability means proving it, not just doing it.'
cards.back: Fact. Article 5(2) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance.

cards.front: 'Business contact details of a sole trader can be personal data.'
cards.back: Fact. A sole trader is a living individual, so data about them is personal data.

cards.title: What getting it wrong can cost
cards.caption: Maximums from UK GDPR Article 83 and DPA 2018 section 157. Bank regulators can fine separately for systems and controls failures.

items.label: Higher maximum
items.detail: Or 4% of worldwide annual turnover if higher, e.g. for breaching the core principles.

items.label: Standard maximum
items.detail: Or 2% of turnover if higher, e.g. for many security and record duties.

items.label: Equifax Ltd (FCA, 2023)
items.detail: FCA penalty for failing to oversee outsourced UK data.

items.label: UK consumers affected
items.detail: Approximate number in the Equifax case, per the FCA.

cards.question: Harrowfield sends customer data to a group company in another country for processing. Which statement is correct?
options: Responsibility passes to the group company once the data leaves the UK
Intra-group transfers are exempt from data protection rules
Harrowfield remains responsible as controller and must oversee how the data is protected
Only the group company's regulator can take action if data is lost
cards.explanation: The controller stays accountable for data it sends to processors, including group companies. The Equifax case shows that failing to treat a parent company as an outsourcing provider, and failing to oversee it, can lead to enforcement.

cards.title: Back to this morning's two incidents
cards.body:
Both incidents from the opening scene are **personal data breaches in the making**: the emailed customer list is an unauthorised disclosure, and the lost laptop may be one.

- Do not wait for proof of harm. Report to the DPO and the incident line at once.
- Never forward customer data to personal email or devices, even 'to work on at home'.
- Encryption may change the risk assessment, but only if the device was locked and the key is safe.

You will learn the breach rules in Stage 4.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: UK data protection law rests on the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, both amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
The Information Commission replaced the Information Commissioner (ICO) on 30 September 2026; the FCA and PRA also police data security as a systems and controls issue.
Personal data is any information about an identifiable living person; in a bank that is almost every record.
Article 5 sets six principles plus accountability: the bank must be able to prove compliance.
Sending data to a supplier or group company does not transfer the controller's responsibility.

cards.prompt: Think of one set of customer data you use every week. What is its purpose, which fields do you actually need, and when should it be deleted? Who could you ask if you do not know?

quiz.question: Which pair of laws forms the core of UK data protection law for a bank, as amended in 2025?
options: The EU GDPR and the Data Protection Act 1998
The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
The Data Protection Act 2018 and the Financial Services Act 2021
The Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations alone
quiz.explanation: The UK GDPR and the DPA 2018 work together, and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended both. The 1998 Act was replaced, and the EU GDPR no longer applies directly in the UK.

quiz.question: Since 30 September 2026, which body enforces UK data protection law?
options: The Information Commissioner's Office, unchanged
The Financial Conduct Authority
The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
The Information Commission
quiz.explanation: Commencement regulations under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 abolished the office of Information Commissioner and transferred its functions to the Information Commission from 30 September 2026.

quiz.question: A branch keeps a CCTV recording in which customers' faces are visible. How should staff treat it?
options: As personal data, because individuals can be identified from the images
As non-personal data, because no names are attached
As personal data only if the footage is shared outside the bank
As anonymous data once it is older than one month
quiz.explanation: Images from which people can be identified are personal data whether or not names are attached. Sharing and age do not change that.

quiz.question: Harrowfield uses a cloud provider to host its mortgage system. The provider only acts on the bank's instructions. What is the provider's role?
options: Joint controller
Data subject
Processor
Controller
quiz.explanation: A firm that processes personal data on behalf of, and on the instructions of, the controller is a processor. The bank decides the purposes and means, so it remains the controller.

quiz.question: A credit team keeps the full application files of rejected applicants indefinitely 'in case they reapply'. Which principle is most at risk?
options: Accuracy
Lawfulness of the original collection
Storage limitation
Transparency of the privacy notice
quiz.explanation: Keeping identifiable data for longer than the purpose requires breaches storage limitation. The files may be accurate and lawfully collected, but there is no defined need to keep them forever.

quiz.question: What does the accountability principle in UK GDPR Article 5(2) add to the other principles?
options: The controller must be responsible for compliance and able to demonstrate it
Each member of staff becomes personally liable to a fine for any breach of the principles
The DPO must sign off every processing activity in advance
The regulator must approve the bank's privacy policy
quiz.explanation: Accountability makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance with the principles, for example through records, policies, assessments and training evidence. It does not create personal fines for staff or a pre-approval regime.

quiz.question: The marketing team asks for the fraud team's list of customers flagged in fraud checks, to target them with a 'security upgrade' product. What is the main problem?
options: The fraud team cannot share any data with any other team in any circumstances whatsoever
The list is not personal data because it is internal
Marketing is never a lawful purpose for a bank
Reusing fraud-check data for marketing is likely incompatible with its original purpose
quiz.explanation: Purpose limitation stops data collected for one purpose from being reused in an incompatible way. Internal sharing can be lawful in other cases, and marketing can be lawful with the right basis, but this reuse is the issue.

quiz.question: Which statement about special category data is correct?
options: It means any financial data, such as balances, salaries and loan amounts, which the law treats as especially sensitive
It covers sensitive types such as health data and needs an additional condition as well as a lawful basis
It can never be processed by a bank
It only applies to data about children
quiz.explanation: Special category data includes health, ethnic origin, religious belief and biometric data used for identification. It needs a lawful basis and a separate condition. Financial data is sensitive in practice but is not a special category in law.

quiz.question: In the Equifax Ltd case (FCA, 2023), what was a central failing?
options: It did not treat sending UK data to its US parent as outsourcing, so did not oversee it
It sold UK customer data to marketing firms without telling consumers or asking for their consent first
It refused to answer subject access requests for two years
It kept paper files in an unlocked office
quiz.explanation: The FCA found that Equifax Ltd did not treat the arrangement with its parent as outsourcing and did not properly oversee the security of UK data sent to US servers, which hackers reached in 2017.

quiz.question: Under UK GDPR Article 83, what is the higher maximum fine for an undertaking that breaches the core processing principles?
options: GBP 8.7m or 2% of UK turnover, whichever is lower
GBP 500,000 per breach
GBP 17.5m or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
1% of the bank's capital requirement
quiz.explanation: Breaches of the basic principles fall under the higher maximum: GBP 17.5m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for the preceding year, whichever is higher. The GBP 8.7m or 2% standard maximum applies to other provisions.

sessions.title: Lawful Bases, Recognised Legitimate Interests and Customer Confidentiality
sessions.summary: Choose the right lawful basis, use the new recognised legitimate interests added by the 2025 Act, apply the banker's duty of confidentiality, and avoid the DPA 2018 section 170 offence.
objectives: Select the right Article 6 lawful basis for common banking activities
Distinguish recognised legitimate interests from ordinary legitimate interests
Apply the duty of confidentiality to third-party and authority requests
Explain the section 170 offence and why access logs matter

cards.title: The caller who 'just needs an address'
cards.setting: Contact centre, Harrowfield Bank, Edinburgh. Tuesday, 10:15 am.

lines.text: Nadia, a man on line 4 says he's the husband of one of our customers. She's moved out and he 'just needs her new address to send her post'. He knows her date of birth and account number.
Knowing her details doesn't make him her. And even a real husband has no right to her address.
Then an hour ago a police officer emailed asking for a different customer's statements. Same answer?
Not necessarily. The police request may have a lawful route. The husband's request has none. The difference is the lawful basis, and our duty of confidentiality.
And note what happened: someone who isn't the customer already had her account number and date of birth. That's a warning sign in itself.
Stage 2, then: when can the bank use or share personal data at all, and when must it say no?

cards.title: Seven doors to lawful processing

scenes.heading: One door is enough, but you need one
scenes.narration: Under UK GDPR Article 6, processing is lawful only if at least one lawful basis applies. Pick it before you start, and record it.

scenes.heading: Consent and contract
scenes.narration: Consent must be specific and freely given. Contract covers what is necessary to run an account or loan the customer asked for, including steps before signing.

scenes.heading: Legal obligation and vital interests
scenes.narration: Legal obligation covers what the law makes the bank do, such as anti-money laundering checks. Vital interests is for life-or-death situations.

scenes.heading: Public task
scenes.narration: Public task mainly serves public bodies carrying out official functions. Banks rarely rely on it for their own processing.

scenes.heading: Recognised legitimate interests
scenes.narration: The 2025 Act added a new basis: a short list of purposes, such as crime prevention, safeguarding vulnerable people and emergencies, that Parliament has already judged legitimate.

scenes.heading: Legitimate interests
scenes.narration: Ordinary legitimate interests need a balancing test: the bank's interest must not be overridden by the person's rights, especially if they are a child.

cards.title: Legitimate interests vs recognised legitimate interests

items.label: Where it comes from
items.right: Article 6(1)(ea) and Annex 1, added by the 2025 Act

items.label: Balancing test
items.left: Needed: weigh the interest against the person's rights
items.right: Not needed for the listed purposes

items.label: What purposes
items.left: Any genuine interest, e.g. direct marketing or network security
items.right: Only listed ones, e.g. crime, safeguarding, emergencies, national security

cards.question: Under the 2025 changes, which of these purposes is listed in Annex 1 as a recognised legitimate interest?
options: Processing necessary to send personalised mortgage offers
Processing necessary to improve the bank's app design
Processing necessary to share data with any group company
Processing necessary to detect, investigate or prevent crime
cards.explanation: Annex 1 lists purposes including crime detection and prevention, safeguarding vulnerable individuals, emergencies, national security and certain disclosures to public bodies. Marketing and intra-group sharing are given as examples of ordinary legitimate interests, which still need a balancing test.

cards.title: Which lawful basis fits best?
cards.prompt: Sort each Harrowfield activity to the lawful basis that fits it best.

items.text: Processing a customer's standing order instruction
Checking identity under the money laundering rules
Running the fraud-detection model on card payments
Sending a statement for the current account
Answering a court order for account records
Monitoring the network for malware
Assessing a loan application the customer submitted
Alerting social services about a vulnerable adult at risk of harm

cards.title: Customer confidentiality: the older, stricter duty
cards.body:
Long before UK GDPR, UK banks owed customers a **duty of confidentiality** that comes from the banker-customer relationship itself. Data protection sits on top of it, not in place of it.

In practice this means:

- A customer's affairs are not discussed with anyone else, including spouses, parents, employers or friends, unless the customer has authorised it or another recognised exception applies.
- Exceptions are **narrow**: for example, where the law compels disclosure, or where the customer has clearly agreed. Your bank's policy lists them.
- Requests from police or other authorities go to the **designated team**, which checks the legal basis, the scope and the paperwork.

If a request feels unusual, the safe answer is: 'I can't discuss any account, but I can pass your request to the right team.'

cards.title: Handling a request for customer information
cards.caption: Never confirm or deny that someone is a customer until the first two steps are done.

items.label: Verify who is asking
items.detail: Use the bank's verification steps; knowing details is not proof.

items.label: Check their authority
items.detail: Is it the customer, an authorised third party or a body with a legal power?

items.label: Identify the lawful route
items.detail: Lawful basis, confidentiality exception and policy all need to line up.

items.label: Share the minimum
items.detail: Only what is needed for that purpose.

items.label: Record the decision
items.detail: Who asked, what was shared, why, and who approved it.

cards.title: The turn: the curious colleague
cards.setting: HR meeting room, Leeds. Tuesday, 3 pm.

lines.text: Bad news. An audit of system logs shows a payments clerk viewed his ex-partner's account 14 times last month. No business reason.
Looking without a business reason is unauthorised processing. If he passed anything on, it could be a criminal offence for him personally.
Under the Data Protection Act?
Section 170. Knowingly or recklessly obtaining or disclosing personal data without the controller's consent. The bank never consented to him browsing.
My team must hear this. Some of them look up neighbours 'just out of curiosity'.

cards.title: The police email
cards.situation: A message arrives at the Edinburgh contact centre from an address ending in .police.uk. It asks for six months of statements for a named customer 'urgently, for an ongoing fraud investigation' and gives an officer's name. The customer is not under any internal investigation.

choices.text: Do not send anything; log the request and pass it to the bank's designated disclosure team, which will verify it and check the legal basis and scope
choices.outcome: Best answer. Crime prevention can be a lawful purpose, but the bank must verify the requester, check the legal basis and confidentiality exception, and share only what is necessary. Specialist teams exist for exactly this.

choices.text: Send the statements, because crime prevention is a recognised legitimate interest
choices.outcome: The recognised legitimate interest still requires the processing to be necessary, and confidentiality and verification rules still apply. A contact-centre agent cannot make that judgement alone.

choices.text: Phone the customer to ask whether they agree to the disclosure
choices.outcome: Contacting the customer could prejudice a genuine investigation. The request should go to the specialist team, which knows how to handle it.

choices.text: Reply that the bank never shares data with police
choices.outcome: Wrong. The bank can lawfully share data with law enforcement in the right circumstances. The answer is a controlled process, not a blanket refusal.

cards.title: Rules and their sources
cards.prompt: Match each rule to where it comes from.

pairs.right: At least one lawful basis is needed for any processing.
Lists the recognised legitimate interests, such as safeguarding and crime.
Gives examples of ordinary legitimate interests: direct marketing, intra-group admin, network security.
Offence of knowingly or recklessly obtaining or disclosing data without the controller's consent.
Banker-customer duty not to disclose a customer's affairs except in narrow cases.

cards.question: A payments clerk looks up his ex-partner's balance out of curiosity and tells a friend. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is only a disciplinary matter, because he had system access
He may have committed an offence under DPA 2018 section 170, and the bank should treat it as a breach
It is lawful because he did not change any data
Only the bank can be liable; staff never face personal consequences
cards.explanation: Section 170 makes it an offence for a person knowingly or recklessly to obtain or disclose personal data without the controller's consent. Having system access is not consent to use it for private reasons. The bank must also assess it as a personal data breach.

cards.title: Confidentiality quick answers

cards.front: A wife asks for her husband's balance 'because it's a joint mortgage'.
cards.back: Only discuss accounts she is party to or authorised on. A joint mortgage does not open his sole current account.

cards.front: A caller knows the account number and date of birth.
cards.back: That is not verification. Fraudsters often hold such details. Use the bank's full verification steps.

cards.front: An employer asks to confirm a salary deposit.
cards.back: Only with the customer's documented authority, through the agreed reference process.

cards.front: A solicitor says they act for the customer.
cards.back: Ask for written authority signed by the customer and route it through the proper team.

cards.front: Can I check a friend's account to help them?
cards.back: No. Access is for assigned work only. Ask the friend to contact the bank in the usual way.

cards.title: Real case lesson: why access logs matter (FCA, Tesco Bank, 2018)
cards.body:
Confidentiality failures are often found in the **logs**. In its October 2018 final notice against **Tesco Personal Finance plc**, fined about **GBP 16.4m** over a November 2016 cyber attack on debit cards, the FCA set out, hour by hour, what each team did and failed to do.

That case was about fraud, not snooping, and no customer personal data was lost. But it shows how closely a regulator examines **who did what, and when**. At Harrowfield, every look-up you make is logged with your user ID and the time.

At Harrowfield, regular access reviews flag unusual patterns, such as staff viewing colleagues', relatives' or celebrities' accounts. If you need to view an account where you have a personal link, declare it and ask a colleague to handle it.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Every processing activity needs at least one of the lawful bases in UK GDPR Article 6, chosen in advance and recorded.
The 2025 Act added recognised legitimate interests (Annex 1), such as crime prevention, safeguarding and emergencies, with no balancing test; necessity still applies.
Ordinary legitimate interests need a balancing test; direct marketing, intra-group admin and network security are listed examples.
Banks owe customers a duty of confidentiality on top of data protection law; exceptions are narrow and handled by designated teams.
Browsing or disclosing data without a business reason can be a criminal offence under DPA 2018 section 170.

cards.prompt: Which requests for customer information reach you most often? Write down how you verify the requester and which team you pass unusual requests to.

quiz.question: Which lawful basis best fits processing that a customer's current account cannot run without, such as making the payments they instruct?
options: Consent
Vital interests
Public task
Performance of a contract
quiz.explanation: Processing that is necessary to perform a contract with the customer, or to take steps they ask for before entering one, falls under Article 6(1)(b). Consent would be the wrong basis because the customer cannot really refuse it and still have the account.

quiz.question: Why is consent usually a poor lawful basis for identity checks required by money laundering law?
options: The bank must do the checks anyway, so consent would not be freely given; legal obligation fits
Consent is not one of the lawful bases in the UK GDPR, so it cannot be used for any processing by a bank
Consent can only be given in writing on paper
Identity checks need no lawful basis at all
quiz.explanation: Where the law requires processing, the right basis is legal obligation. Asking for consent would be misleading, because the customer cannot refuse without losing the service, so consent would not be freely given.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a recognised legitimate interest and an ordinary legitimate interest?
options: Recognised legitimate interests need the customer's written consent before any processing can start
Ordinary legitimate interests can be used only by public authorities carrying out official tasks for the state
They are listed purposes with no balancing test, though necessity still applies
Recognised legitimate interests remove the need to keep any records
quiz.explanation: Article 6(1)(ea) and Annex 1 list purposes, such as crime prevention and safeguarding, that do not need the balancing test of Article 6(1)(f). Necessity still applies, and the accountability duties are unchanged.

quiz.question: Which of these does UK GDPR Article 6(11) give as an example of processing that may be necessary for an ordinary legitimate interest?
options: Safeguarding a vulnerable individual
Ensuring the security of network and information systems
Responding to a national emergency
Complying with a court order
quiz.explanation: Article 6(11) lists direct marketing, intra-group transmission for internal administration and network and information security as examples of legitimate interests. Safeguarding and emergencies are recognised legitimate interests in Annex 1, and court orders fall under legal obligation.

quiz.question: A caller gives a customer's full name, account number and date of birth and asks for her new address. He says he is her husband. What should the agent do?
options: Decline to discuss her account; knowing details is not verification
Give the address, because he passed the security questions and says he is her husband
Give the town but not the street, so that he can forward her post
Confirm that she is a customer but say nothing more about her account or address
quiz.explanation: Holding someone's details does not prove identity or authority, and the duty of confidentiality covers spouses. Even confirming that she is a customer discloses information.

quiz.question: Under DPA 2018 section 170, which act can be a criminal offence for an individual employee?
options: Making a typing error in a customer's address
Following a manager's lawful instruction to share data with an auditor
Forgetting to read the privacy notice
Knowingly or recklessly disclosing personal data without the controller's consent
quiz.explanation: Section 170 targets knowingly or recklessly obtaining, disclosing, procuring or retaining personal data without the controller's consent. Honest mistakes and authorised sharing are not covered by the offence.

quiz.question: A police officer emails a contact-centre agent asking for a customer's statements for a fraud inquiry. What is the right first step?
options: Send the statements straight away, because crime prevention is always a lawful reason to share
Pass the request to the designated disclosure team to verify it and check the legal basis
Call the customer to ask for permission
Delete the email, because the bank never shares any customer data with the police
quiz.explanation: Disclosures to law enforcement can be lawful, but they need verification, a legal basis, a confidentiality exception and a minimal scope. Calling the customer could prejudice an investigation, and blanket refusal is also wrong.

quiz.question: Which statement about the banker's duty of confidentiality is correct?
options: It was abolished when the UK GDPR took effect, so data protection law is now the only rule
It applies only to business customers
It sits alongside data protection law and allows disclosure only in narrow circumstances
It allows disclosure to any family member who can show they live with the customer
quiz.explanation: The duty of confidentiality comes from the banker-customer relationship and continues alongside UK GDPR and the DPA 2018. Exceptions, such as legal compulsion or the customer's agreement, are narrow.

quiz.question: Harrowfield wants to share customer details with an adult social care team because a customer appears to be at risk of financial abuse. Which basis is most relevant after the 2025 changes?
options: Performance of the customer's account contract, since the bank must run the account safely
Consent from the person suspected of the abuse
No basis is needed for safeguarding because it is always in the customer's interest
The recognised legitimate interest for safeguarding a vulnerable individual
quiz.explanation: Annex 1 includes processing necessary for safeguarding a vulnerable individual, which includes adults at risk. The bank must still judge necessity and share only what is needed, following its vulnerable customer and confidentiality policies.

quiz.question: An adviser has to work on the account of her own cousin, who has walked into her branch. What is the best practice?
options: Declare the personal link and ask a colleague to handle the account
Handle it herself, since she knows the cousin well
Handle it but avoid writing notes
Look at the account first to decide whether a conflict exists
quiz.explanation: Where staff have a personal connection, good practice is to declare it and pass the work to a colleague. Viewing the account first would itself be access without a clear business need.

sessions.title: Data Subject Rights, Automated Decisions and the New Complaints Duty
sessions.summary: Handle access, erasure, objection and other rights on the amended clocks, apply the new automated decision-making rules, and meet the DPA 2018 section 164A complaints duty in force since June 2026.
objectives: Explain each data subject right and its main limits for a bank
Apply the Article 12A response periods, extensions and clock pauses
Recognise solely automated significant decisions and provide the required safeguards
Handle data protection complaints in line with DPA 2018 section 164A

cards.title: The customer who wants 'everything'
cards.setting: Data Protection Office, Leeds. Wednesday, 9:05 am.

lines.text: Nadia, a customer whose loan was declined has emailed: 'Send me every piece of data you hold about me. And I want to know why a computer said no.'
That's a subject access request, and a question about automated decision-making. Both have clocks and rules.
He's also furious. He says if he doesn't hear back he'll complain to the regulator and the newspapers.
Since June 2026 he has a legal right to complain to us first, and we must acknowledge it within 30 days. Let's not give him two reasons to be angry.
Remind me: how long do we have for the data itself? And do we really need to search every inbox in the bank?
Good questions, and the 2025 Act changed some of the answers. Stage 3: people's rights, the clocks and the new complaints duty.

cards.title: The rights every customer holds

scenes.heading: To be informed
scenes.narration: People must be told, in clear and plain language, who is using their data, why, on what basis, for how long and what their rights are. That is the privacy notice's job.

scenes.heading: Of access
scenes.narration: People can ask whether the bank processes their data and get a copy, plus key information such as purposes, recipients and how long it is kept.

scenes.heading: To rectification and erasure
scenes.narration: They can have wrong data corrected, and in some cases deleted. But erasure has limits: data the law requires the bank to keep, such as money laundering records, stays.

scenes.heading: To restrict and to object
scenes.narration: They can ask the bank to pause use while a dispute is checked, and object to processing based on legitimate interests. An objection to direct marketing must always be obeyed.

scenes.heading: About automated decisions
scenes.narration: Where a significant decision is made solely by automated means, the bank must offer safeguards: information, a way to make representations, human intervention and a way to contest it.

cards.title: The clock on a rights request (UK GDPR Articles 12 and 12A)
cards.caption: Inserted by section 76 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Check your bank's procedure for how it counts days.

items.label: Relevant time
items.detail: The latest of: request received, ID information received, or any allowed fee paid.

items.label: Ask for clarification
items.detail: For an access request, if the bank reasonably needs more detail to find the data, the clock stops until it arrives.

items.label: Standard deadline
items.detail: Respond without undue delay and within one month of the relevant time.

items.label: Extension notice
items.detail: If requests are complex or numerous, tell the person, with reasons, before the first month ends.

items.label: Extended deadline
items.detail: The response period can be extended by two further months.

cards.question: A customer submits an access request on 3 March. The bank has reasonable doubts about identity and asks for ID, which arrives on 10 March. When does the one-month period start?
options: When the identity information arrives on 10 March
On 3 March, when the request arrived
When the DPO first reads the request
When the bank finishes its search
cards.explanation: Article 12A starts the clock at the relevant time: the latest of receiving the request, receiving information requested to confirm identity, or payment of any allowed fee. Here that is 10 March.

cards.title: Access requests: what the 2025 Act changed
cards.body:
Subject access requests (SARs) are the most common right used against banks, often during disputes. Three points changed or were clarified in 2025:

- **Reasonable and proportionate search.** People are entitled to what the bank can find through a reasonable and proportionate search. That is not a licence to skip obvious places such as the CRM, call recordings or the complaint file.
- **Clarification.** If the bank holds a lot of data about the person, it may ask which information or activities the request covers, and the clock pauses until the answer arrives.
- **Identity.** Where there is reasonable doubt, the bank may ask for ID and wait until identity is confirmed.

Unchanged: the first copy is normally **free**. A request that is manifestly unfounded or excessive can be refused or charged a reasonable fee, but the bank must be able to prove that it is.

cards.title: Can the bank refuse or delete?
cards.prompt: Sort each request: must the bank normally comply, or may it decline (with reasons)?

items.text: Stop sending me marketing emails.
Correct my misspelt surname.
Delete my transaction history from last year while my account is open.
Send me a copy of my personal data.
Delete the identity documents you hold under money laundering law.
Explain the logic of the automated decision that declined my card.
Send me the 5th identical access request this month.
Pause use of my address while you check whether it's wrong.

cards.title: Automated decisions after the 2025 Act (Articles 22A to 22D)

items.label: When the rules bite
items.right: Legal or similarly significant effect, no meaningful human involvement

items.label: Ordinary personal data
items.right: Inform, allow representations, human intervention, contest

items.label: Special category data
items.right: Only with explicit consent, or contract or law plus a public interest condition

items.label: Recognised legitimate interests
items.right: Solely automated significant decisions cannot rely on Article 6(1)(ea)

cards.title: The turn: the complaint form nobody could find

lines.text: Mystery shopping result: a tester tried to complain online that we'd shared her data wrongly. The only route was a phone line, open on weekdays.
That's a problem. Section 164A of the 2018 Act now says controllers must make complaining easy, for example with a form that works electronically and by other means.
And after the complaint comes in?
Acknowledge within 30 days, look into it properly, keep the person updated and tell them the outcome without undue delay.
Our general complaints process already does most of that. Can we just plug data complaints into it?
Yes, if we tag them, involve my team, and track the 30-day acknowledgement. The regulator can fine for breaching section 164A.

cards.title: Handling a data protection complaint under DPA 2018 s.164A
steps: Make it easy to complain, with an electronic form and other routes
Log the complaint and tag it as a data protection complaint
Acknowledge receipt within 30 days of receiving it
Make appropriate enquiries into what happened
Keep the complainant informed of progress
Tell the complainant the outcome without undue delay

cards.title: The angry declined applicant
cards.situation: The declined loan applicant from this morning has now emailed three times: an access request, a demand to know 'why the computer said no', and a complaint that the bank 'is hiding something'. Harrowfield's lending decision was made by a scoring engine with no human review. Eilidh asks you how to respond.

choices.text: Log the access request and the complaint, acknowledge the complaint, explain the decision safeguards and offer human review, then answer within the applicable time limits
choices.outcome: Best answer. A solely automated significant decision triggers safeguards: information, a chance to make representations, human intervention and a route to contest. The access request has its own clock and the complaint must be acknowledged within 30 days.

choices.text: Reply that scoring models are confidential and nothing can be shared
choices.outcome: Wrong. The person is entitled to meaningful information about the logic and to contest the decision. Trade secrets may limit detail, but not remove the safeguards.

choices.text: Treat it all as one complaint and answer within eight weeks
choices.outcome: Partly right in spirit, but each right has its own rules. The access request has a one-month clock, and the decision safeguards must be offered.

choices.text: Wait for him to complain to the Information Commission before acting
choices.outcome: Risky. Since June 2026 the bank must handle complaints itself, and delay could breach both the access and the complaint rules.

cards.title: Rights: sharp edges

cards.front: Is the first copy of an access request free?
cards.back: Normally yes. A reasonable fee is possible for further copies, or for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests.

cards.front: Can the bank refuse an access request because the person is in a dispute with it?
cards.back: Not on that ground alone. The right of access has no motive test, and the bank bears the burden of showing a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive.

cards.front: Must an objection to direct marketing be obeyed?
cards.back: Yes. Data must no longer be processed for direct marketing once the person objects.

cards.front: Does erasure override money laundering record-keeping?
cards.back: No. Erasure does not apply where processing is needed to comply with a legal obligation.

cards.front: What must the bank say if it does not act on a request?
cards.back: Give its reasons and tell the person they can complain to the bank, to the Information Commission and seek a court remedy.

cards.title: Real case: complaints mishandled after a breach (FCA, Equifax Ltd, 2023)
cards.body:
The FCA's 2023 penalty against **Equifax Ltd** was not only about security. It also found that:

- Equifax Ltd was told about the incident only about **five minutes** before its US parent announced it, so it could not cope with the complaints that followed.
- It made public statements that gave an **inaccurate impression of how many UK consumers** were affected.
- It treated consumers unfairly by failing to keep **quality checks on complaints**, so complaints were mishandled.

**The lesson for Harrowfield:** rights requests and complaints spike after an incident. A complaints process that works on a quiet Tuesday must also work on the worst day of the year. Since June 2026, handling data protection complaints is also a statutory duty under DPA 2018 section 164A.

cards.question: Under DPA 2018 section 164A, which is a duty of the bank when it receives a data protection complaint?
options: Acknowledge receipt within 30 days and tell the complainant the outcome without undue delay
Resolve the complaint within 72 hours
Forward every complaint to the Information Commission
Respond only if the complaint is in writing on paper
cards.explanation: Section 164A, in force from 19 June 2026, requires controllers to facilitate complaints (for example with an electronic form), acknowledge them within 30 days, make appropriate enquiries, keep the person informed and tell them the outcome without undue delay.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Rights: to be informed, access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection and safeguards on solely automated significant decisions.
Rights requests: one month from the relevant time, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests with notice and reasons in the first month.
Access requests: a reasonable and proportionate search, the clock pauses for clarification, and the first copy is normally free.
Solely automated significant decisions need safeguards: information, representations, human intervention and a right to contest.
Since 19 June 2026, DPA 2018 s.164A requires an easy complaint route, acknowledgement within 30 days and an outcome without undue delay.

cards.prompt: If a customer phoned you today asking for 'all my data', what would you say, who would you pass it to, and how would you record the date?

quiz.question: What is the standard time limit for responding to a data subject's access request under the UK GDPR as amended?
options: 40 calendar days from receipt, with no possibility of extension in any case
72 hours from receipt
One month from the relevant time, extendable by two months in some cases
Eight weeks, in line with the bank's general complaints timetable
quiz.explanation: Article 12A sets one month from the relevant time, which can be extended by two further months where requests are complex or numerous, with notice and reasons given within the first month.

quiz.question: Harrowfield receives a complex access request covering ten years of records. It wants more time. What must it do?
options: Simply respond late, because complex requests have no fixed deadline under the amended rules
Notify the customer, with reasons, before the first month ends
Ask the Information Commission for permission to extend the period
Charge a fee before starting the search
quiz.explanation: The bank may extend by two further months for complexity or number of requests, but it must give notice with reasons within the first month of the relevant time.

quiz.question: A long-standing customer asks for all the data the bank holds. Which statement about the search reflects the 2025 changes?
options: The bank need only search the CRM system
The bank must search every system, archive and backup tape regardless of effort
The bank can refuse because it holds too much data
The customer is entitled to what the bank can find through a reasonable and proportionate search
quiz.explanation: Article 15(1A) limits entitlement to what a reasonable and proportionate search can find. That still covers the obvious places, but it does not require disproportionate effort, and volume alone is not a reason to refuse.

quiz.question: A customer objects to the bank using her data for direct marketing. What must the bank do?
options: Stop processing her data for direct marketing
Weigh its commercial interest against her objection
Continue until her next annual review
Ask her to give a reason before acting
quiz.explanation: An objection to direct marketing is absolute under Article 21(2) and (3). No balancing test or reason is needed.

quiz.question: A customer asks the bank to erase the identity documents it collected when he opened an account two years ago. The account is still open. What is the best answer?
options: The bank must erase them within one month, because the customer has an absolute right to erasure
Decline erasure, explaining that the law requires the bank to keep them
The bank must erase them only if he pays a fee
The bank should erase them now and ask him to send new copies of his documents later
quiz.explanation: Erasure does not apply where processing is needed to comply with a legal obligation, such as money laundering record-keeping. The bank must explain its reasons and the person's complaint and remedy options.

quiz.question: Which situation triggers the safeguards for automated decision-making in Articles 22A to 22C?
options: A human underwriter reviews a score and makes the final decision with real authority
A system sorts emails into folders for staff
A credit card is declined by a scoring engine with no meaningful human involvement
A customer uses an online calculator to estimate loan repayments
quiz.explanation: The safeguards apply to significant decisions, meaning those with legal or similarly significant effects, taken solely by automated processing, which means no meaningful human involvement. A genuine human decision-maker takes it outside the rule.

quiz.question: Which safeguards must the bank provide for a solely automated significant decision?
options: Information, representations, human intervention and a way to contest
A refund of any fees charged and a written apology from a senior manager
A guarantee that the decision will be reversed whenever the person asks for it
Only a copy of the privacy notice
quiz.explanation: Article 22C requires measures that inform the person, let them make representations, obtain human intervention and contest the decision. It does not require the decision to be reversed.

quiz.question: From 19 June 2026, how quickly must a controller acknowledge a data protection complaint under DPA 2018 section 164A?
options: Within 72 hours
Within one month of the outcome
Within eight weeks
Within 30 days of receiving it
quiz.explanation: Section 164A(3) requires acknowledgement within the period of 30 days beginning when the complaint is received. The outcome must then follow without undue delay.

quiz.question: A customer who is in a dispute with the bank makes an access request to gather evidence. The branch manager wants to refuse it as 'manifestly unfounded'. What is the best advice?
options: Refuse, because access rights cannot be used to gather evidence while a dispute with the bank is still open
Do not refuse because of the dispute; the bank must be able to show it is unfounded or excessive
Refuse, but only after the dispute is settled
Comply only if the customer agrees in writing to drop the dispute first
quiz.explanation: The right of access contains no motive test, so a dispute does not by itself make a request unfounded. Article 12(5) puts the burden of demonstrating that a request is manifestly unfounded or excessive on the controller.

quiz.question: When the bank decides not to act on a rights request, what must it tell the person?
options: Nothing, as long as it records the decision and its reasons in the internal case file
Only that the request has been closed and will not be reopened
Its reasons, and its routes to complain to the bank or regulator and to the courts
That they must wait 12 months before asking again, and that any repeat request will be charged a fee by the bank
quiz.explanation: Article 12(4) requires the controller to explain why it is not acting and to tell the person about complaining to the controller under s.164A, complaining to the regulator under s.165 and seeking a judicial remedy.

sessions.title: Security, Social Engineering and Breach Notification
sessions.summary: Apply UK GDPR Article 32 security duties, resist phishing and pretexting, and run the Article 33 and 34 breach process: record every breach, notify the Information Commission within 72 hours where required and tell customers when risk is high.
objectives: Describe the security measures UK GDPR Article 32 expects
Recognise phishing, pretexting and payment diversion attempts and respond safely
Decide whether a breach must be recorded, notified to the regulator or communicated to customers
Learn from the Tesco Bank and Equifax enforcement cases

cards.title: 16:52: the email from the 'COO'
cards.setting: Cyber Security Operations, Harrowfield Bank, Leeds. Thursday, 4:52 pm.

lines.text: Alert. Three staff in Finance got an email 'from Helen' asking them to open a 'board pack' link and log in. One of them did.
I sent nothing. And I never ask anyone to log in through a link.
The login page was fake. The attacker now has a valid password, and that mailbox holds customer complaint files with names, addresses and account details.
Then the clock may already be running. If personal data has been accessed, we have a possible notifiable breach.
And if the attacker pivots into payment systems, it's an operational incident too. Two sets of rules, one bad afternoon.
Stage 4: security, social engineering, and what the law makes us do in the hours after a breach.

cards.title: Security in the UK GDPR, Article 32

scenes.heading: Appropriate to the risk
scenes.narration: The bank must use technical and organisational measures that match the risk to people, taking account of cost, the state of the art and what the data is used for.

scenes.heading: Encryption and pseudonymisation
scenes.narration: Encrypting data and replacing identifiers with codes are named examples. They make stolen data much less useful to a thief.

scenes.heading: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, resilience
scenes.narration: Systems must stay confidential, accurate, available and resilient on an ongoing basis, and the bank must be able to restore access to data quickly after an incident.

scenes.heading: Test it regularly
scenes.narration: Controls must be tested, assessed and evaluated regularly. A control nobody has tested is a hope, not a control.

scenes.heading: People act on instructions
scenes.narration: Anyone with access to personal data may process it only on the controller's instructions. Training and clear rules turn that duty into daily habit.

cards.title: Technical and organisational measures
cards.caption: Article 32 needs both: strong technology fails if people are tricked, and good people fail without tools.

items.label: Encryption
items.detail: Laptops, emails with attachments and backups encrypted by default.

items.label: Access control
items.detail: Least privilege, multi-factor login and regular access reviews.

items.label: Training and awareness
items.detail: Phishing drills, clear desk rules and a no-blame reporting culture.

items.label: Procedures
items.detail: Verification scripts, call-back rules and secure disposal of paper.

cards.title: Social engineering: red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each message or call that reaches Harrowfield staff.

items.text: An email from 'the CEO' asks you to log in via a link to read board papers
A supplier emails new bank details for its next invoice payment
A caller from 'IT support' asks for your one-time passcode to fix your account
A text from 'the bank's fraud team' asks a customer to move money to a 'safe account'
The IT service desk ticket you raised is updated in the official ticketing tool
A colleague asks you to leave a door propped open because they forgot their pass
Your manager reminds you in a team meeting about the annual policy attestation
A new customer's documents arrive through the secure upload portal you sent them

cards.title: Five habits that beat phishing and pretexting
cards.body:
Good practice, not a statutory checklist:

- **Pause on urgency.** Pressure, secrecy and authority ('the CEO needs this now') are the attacker's tools.
- **Verify out of band.** Call back on a number from the bank's directory, never one in the message.
- **Never share codes or passwords.** No genuine colleague, supplier or bank team needs your one-time passcode.
- **Check payment changes twice.** New bank details for a supplier or customer are confirmed by a call-back to a known contact.
- **Report fast, without fear.** Clicking is a mistake; hiding it is the real damage. Use the phishing report button at once.

cards.question: A supplier emails to say its bank details have changed and asks Harrowfield to pay this month's invoice to the new account. What is the best response?
options: Confirm the change by calling the supplier on a number already held on file before updating anything
Reply to the email asking the supplier to confirm
Update the details, because the email comes from the supplier's usual address
Pay half to the old account and half to the new one
cards.explanation: Email accounts can be compromised or spoofed, so a reply goes to the attacker. Out-of-band verification with a known contact is the standard defence against payment diversion fraud.

cards.title: What counts as a personal data breach
cards.body:
A **personal data breach** is a security breach that leads to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data.

It is wider than hacking:

- **Confidentiality**: a customer list emailed to the wrong person or a personal address; a phished mailbox.
- **Integrity**: someone changes payment details or balances without authority.
- **Availability**: ransomware locks customer files, or records are destroyed without a backup.

Not every breach is reportable, but **every breach is recorded**. Article 33(5) requires the bank to document all personal data breaches: the facts, their effects and the remedial action, so the regulator can check its decisions.

cards.title: From incident to notification (Articles 33 and 34)
cards.caption: If notification to the regulator comes after 72 hours, it must give the reasons for the delay.

items.label: Security incident
items.detail: Anything that might affect the security of data or systems.

items.label: Personal data breach
items.detail: Personal data destroyed, lost, altered, disclosed or accessed without authority. Record it.

items.label: Risk to people
items.detail: Notify the Information Commission without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness.

items.label: High risk to people
items.detail: Also tell the affected people without undue delay, in clear and plain language.

cards.title: The turn: 'let's wait until we're sure'

lines.text: The attacker read 340 complaint files before we locked the mailbox. Names, addresses, account numbers and some notes about customers' health.
Should we wait until forensics finishes next week? I don't want to report something we don't fully understand.
We don't have to understand everything. Article 33 lets us notify in phases. The 72 hours runs from when we became aware, which was this afternoon.
And with health notes and account numbers, the risk to customers looks high. That means telling them too.
Agreed. Initial notice to the Commission tomorrow morning, then a clear message to the 340 customers with what to watch for.

cards.title: The phished mailbox decision
cards.situation: Forensics confirm that 340 complaint files were viewed by the attacker. They include names, addresses, account numbers and, for some customers, notes about health conditions linked to financial difficulty. The files were not encrypted at rest. It is now 26 hours since the bank became aware.

choices.text: Notify the Information Commission now with what is known, follow up in phases, tell affected customers without undue delay and record everything
choices.outcome: Best answer. There is clearly a risk to people, so notification is needed within 72 hours where feasible, and phased updates are allowed. Health data and account numbers point to high risk, so customers must be told, with practical advice.

choices.text: Notify the Commission but not the customers, to avoid alarming them
choices.outcome: Partly right. Where the risk to people is high, Article 34 requires the bank to tell them without undue delay unless an exception applies. No exception applies to unencrypted files.

choices.text: Wait for the full forensic report next week, then decide
choices.outcome: Wrong. Waiting would almost certainly miss the 72-hour expectation. Notification can be made in phases as facts emerge.

choices.text: Treat it as an IT incident only, because no money was stolen
choices.outcome: Wrong. Unauthorised access to personal data is a personal data breach whether or not money moves.

cards.title: Breach rules in one line each

cards.front: When does the 72-hour period start?
cards.back: When the controller becomes aware of the breach, not when the breach happened or when the investigation ends.

cards.front: What if the bank needs longer than 72 hours?
cards.back: It notifies late with reasons for the delay, and may send information in phases.

cards.front: What must a processor do?
cards.back: Tell the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a breach.

cards.front: When can the bank skip telling customers about a high-risk breach?
cards.back: If the data was made unintelligible (e.g. strong encryption), if later steps remove the high risk, or, with disproportionate effort, by a public notice instead.

cards.front: Must small breaches be recorded?
cards.back: Yes. All personal data breaches are documented, including those not reported.

cards.front: Is notifying the Commission enough for the FCA and PRA?
cards.back: No. Banks must also consider their FCA and PRA notification duties for operational incidents.

cards.title: Real case: Tesco Bank cyber attack (FCA, 2018)
cards.body:
In October 2018 the FCA fined **Tesco Personal Finance plc** about **GBP 16.4m** (about GBP 23.4m before a settlement discount) over a cyber attack on its debit cards in November 2016.

- Attackers made thousands of unauthorised transactions over about **48 hours**, taking about **GBP 2.26m**. No customer personal data was lost.
- The financial crime operations team **emailed a team inbox instead of phoning** the on-call fraud analyst, as procedures required. It took **21 hours** from the start of the attack to reach the fraud strategy team.
- A first blocking rule failed because it used a **currency code instead of a country code**, and nobody checked that it worked.

**The lesson for Harrowfield:** escalation routes, on-call duties and testing of fixes are as important as the technology.

cards.question: Harrowfield's mailing house tells the bank on Monday that it sent 200 statements to the wrong addresses the previous Wednesday. When does the bank's 72-hour period start?
options: When the bank became aware, on Monday
On Wednesday, when the misdelivery happened
When the bank finishes its investigation
There is no period, because the processor made the error
cards.explanation: The controller's 72-hour expectation runs from when it becomes aware of the breach. The processor should have told the bank without undue delay, which is a separate failing for the bank to address with its supplier.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Article 32: security appropriate to the risk, including encryption, ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, timely restoration and regular testing.
Social engineering targets people: pause on urgency, verify out of band, never share codes and report clicks at once.
A personal data breach covers loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data; every breach is documented.
Notify the Information Commission without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness unless the breach is unlikely to cause risk; give reasons if late.
Tell affected people without undue delay when the risk to them is high, unless an Article 34(3) exception applies.

cards.prompt: If you clicked a phishing link tomorrow, exactly how would you report it, and to whom? If you do not know the button or number, find it today.

quiz.question: Which of these is named in UK GDPR Article 32 as an example of an appropriate security measure?
options: Pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data
Publishing staff passwords in a secure binder
Annual deletion of all customer data
Removing all access controls to speed up service
quiz.explanation: Article 32(1)(a) names pseudonymisation and encryption. The article also covers ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, timely restoration and regular testing.

quiz.question: A caller says he is from the bank's IT support and asks an agent for the one-time passcode just sent to her phone 'to fix her login'. What should she do?
options: Give the code, because IT support has authority over all staff systems and accounts
Give only the first half of the code
Refuse, end the call and report it, because no genuine colleague needs her passcode
Ask the caller for his staff number and team name, then give the code once he has answered
quiz.explanation: One-time passcodes must never be shared. A staff number is easy to fake. The right response is to refuse, end the call and report the attempt through the bank's channel.

quiz.question: Which event is a personal data breach under the UK GDPR?
options: A server is patched during a planned maintenance window
Ransomware makes customer records unavailable and there is no usable backup
A phishing email is blocked by the filter before anyone opens it
A customer forgets their own online banking password
quiz.explanation: A breach includes the loss of availability of personal data, not only disclosure. A blocked email or routine maintenance does not affect the security of personal data.

quiz.question: Within what time should a controller notify the regulator of a notifiable personal data breach?
options: Within 24 hours of the breach occurring, whether or not the bank knows about it yet
Within one month, together with any access requests
Only after the investigation is complete and the cause is known
Without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it
quiz.explanation: Article 33(1) requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. Late notifications must give reasons, and information can be provided in phases.

quiz.question: A breach exposed customer names and account numbers, but the bank judges it is unlikely to result in any risk to people. What must the bank still do?
options: Notify the regulator within 72 hours anyway
Notify every customer by letter
Nothing, because unlikely-risk breaches are outside the law
Document the breach, its effects and the remedial action taken
quiz.explanation: Article 33(5) requires all breaches to be documented, including those that are not notified. The documentation must allow the regulator to check the decision.

quiz.question: A laptop holding customer files is stolen. The files were protected with strong encryption and the key was not compromised. Why might the bank not need to tell customers?
options: Stolen laptops are never personal data breaches, because the device rather than the data was taken
The encryption made the data unintelligible, an Article 34(3) exception
Customers only need to be told if money is stolen from their accounts as a direct result of the theft
The police, not the bank, must inform customers
quiz.explanation: If effective measures such as encryption make the data unintelligible to anyone not authorised to access it, the high-risk communication is not required. The bank must still record the breach and assess whether the regulator needs notifying.

quiz.question: Harrowfield's notification to the regulator is made 90 hours after it became aware of a breach. What must the notification include?
options: Nothing extra, since 72 hours is only a guide
A request for permission to notify late
Reasons for the delay, in addition to the required breach information
Proof that customers have already been compensated
quiz.explanation: Where notification is not made within 72 hours, Article 33(1) requires it to be accompanied by reasons for the delay.

quiz.question: In the Tesco Bank case (FCA, 2018), which failing helped the attack run for many hours?
options: Staff emailed a team inbox instead of phoning the on-call fraud analyst
The bank refused to block any transactions at all until the attack ended
Customers' personal data was stolen in the attack and later sold to other criminals online
The bank had no fraud detection system
quiz.explanation: The FCA found that the financial crime operations team emailed the fraud strategy inbox instead of phoning the on-call analyst, and it took 21 hours to reach the specialist team. The bank did have a detection system, and no personal data was lost.

quiz.question: Which statement about notifying people affected by a breach is correct?
options: They must always be told within 72 hours of any breach, whatever the level of risk to them
They only need to be told if the regulator orders it
They must be told without undue delay if the breach is likely to pose a high risk to them
They must be told only if special category data, such as health information, is involved
quiz.explanation: Article 34(1) requires communication to individuals without undue delay when the risk is high. The regulator can also require it, but the duty applies on its own.

quiz.question: What does UK GDPR Article 32(4) require for staff who have access to personal data?
options: They must each register personally with the regulator before they can use any customer data
They process it only on the controller's instructions, unless the law requires otherwise
They may use it for any purpose that helps customers
They must sign a new contract every year
quiz.explanation: Article 32(4) requires controllers and processors to take steps so that people acting under their authority process personal data only on instructions, unless domestic law requires them to do otherwise.

sessions.title: Operational Resilience, Incident Reporting and Your Programme
sessions.summary: Apply PRA and FCA operational resilience rules (important business services, impact tolerances, mapping and testing), prepare for the 2027 incident and third-party reporting regime, and recap the bank's data and resilience programme for the final exam.
objectives: Explain important business services, impact tolerances, mapping, scenario testing and self-assessment
Apply the FCA PS26/2 and PRA PS7/26 incident reporting definition, thresholds and phases
Decide when one event triggers both data breach and operational incident reporting
Describe the roles of the DPO, SMF24, the board and staff, and learn from TSB and other cases

cards.title: Payments are down
cards.setting: Operational Resilience Centre, Harrowfield Bank, Leeds. Friday, 8:10 am.

lines.text: Faster Payments outbound has failed since 7:20. A supplier's update broke the connection. About 60,000 customers can't send money.
Payments is one of our important business services. What's our impact tolerance?
We set it at four hours of disruption at peak. We're 50 minutes in, and the supplier has no fix yet.
Any personal data affected? If transaction data has been corrupted or exposed, my clock starts too.
No sign of that so far. It's an availability problem, not a confidentiality one.
Then let's get it back inside tolerance, and work out who we have to tell. Stage 5, everyone: resilience, reporting and our programme.

cards.title: Operational resilience in five ideas

scenes.heading: Important business services
scenes.narration: A bank identifies the services that, if disrupted, could cause intolerable harm to customers or risk the bank's safety and soundness or the wider system. Payments and access to accounts are typical examples.

scenes.heading: Impact tolerances
scenes.narration: For each important business service, the bank sets the maximum tolerable level of disruption, usually as a time limit. It is a line the bank commits not to cross, not a target to aim for.

scenes.heading: Mapping
scenes.narration: The bank maps the people, processes, technology, facilities, data and third parties that each service depends on, so it can find weak points.

scenes.heading: Severe but plausible scenarios
scenes.narration: The bank tests whether it can stay within tolerance in severe but plausible scenarios, such as a cyber attack or a key supplier failing, and fixes what it finds.

scenes.heading: Self-assessment and board approval
